newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gives car-makers OK to reduce airbag power.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gives car-makers OK to reduce airbag power.

text.p: The U.S. Transportation Department announced on Friday it was allowing car makers to reduce the power of airbags in order to save lives.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said under the new rules, air bags could be de-powered by as much as 35 percent. The reduction in power could be administered immediately, the NHTSA said.
"Safety is our highest priority, and we moved at a record pace to devise an interim solution that can be adopted quickly," NHTSA administrator Ricardo Martinez said in a statment.
While the bags are credited with saving about 1,750 lives since being introduced in the 1980s, their 200 mph (320 kph) inflating force has been blamed for deaths in 62 crashes.

The NHTSA said 38 children had died from fatal injuries caused by airbags. Earlier estimates by the NHTSA have shown that if bags on U.S. cars are reduced in power, 643 lives could be saved annually, although up to 2,000 unbelted drivers and passengers could be killed.
The NHTSA said the new less powerful systems should appear in late model 1997 vehicles or 1998 models.

The NHTSA said the new rule was an interim plan to promote safety. Martinez said a long-term solution was still in the works, including technology to tailor airbag deployment to crash severity, occupant size and position.
